column4: Oftentimes in Christianity we think about repentance as fundamental only to the beginning of our faith in Jesus. The heart of repentance goes much deeper than turning away from sin unto salvation. Repentance from dead works means living with our hearts turned away from the things that harm us or stunt our growth-and turned toward the things of God.
column5: Often in Christianity we consider repentance to be merely a basic thing related to the beginning of our faith. The true spirit of repentance is far deeper than simply turning from sin to obtain salvation. Repentance from dead works means that our heart is turned away from the things that harm us or hinder our growth—and turned toward the things of God.

column4: People may go through a cycle of six stages for change:

column4: 1.  Precontemplation: There is no intention to change.

column4: 2.  Contemplation: There is an intention to change in the near future.
column5: 2.  Contemplation: There is an intention to change in the near future۔

column4: 3.  Preparation: Some steps have been taken to change.
column5: 3.  Preparation: Some steps have been taken toward change۔

column4: 4.  Action: The behavior has been changed for a short time.
column5: 4.  Action: The behavior has been changed for a period of time۔

column4: 5.  Maintenance: The behavior has been changed and continues to be maintained.
column5: 5.  Maintenance: The behavior has changed and is being consistently maintained۔

column4: 6.  Termination: There is no desire to return to the previous behavior.
column5: 6.  Termination: There is no desire to return to the previous behavior۔

column4: There is no set length of time for how long any stage may take. Some people with respect to certain issues in their lives never meaningfully progress through the stages. In other instances, we can progress from stage 1 to 6 very expediently.

column4: ### Godly Sorrow and God’s Goodness
column5: ### Godly Sorrow and the Goodness of God

column4: While hitting rock-bottom is more a myth than a certain precondition to change, God can use sorrow to influence our minds.  God will use sorrow to bring us to repentance. He will convict us of our actions and the state of our lives and hearts to open our eyes to see our complete and total need of Him.
column5: Although hitting rock bottom is less a sure condition for change and more a myth, God can use sorrow to influence our minds. God will use sorrow to bring us to repentance. He will convict us for our actions and for the state of our lives and hearts, so that He may open our eyes and we may see our complete and total need for Him.

column4: Godly sorrow, or <u>the experience of sadness or distress that leads to a *metanoia*</u>, is not the same thing worldly sorrow. Worldly sorrow is the same experience of sadness or distress, but the world offers no hope, only the relief and promise of death.
column5: Godly sorrow, or <u>a grief or distress experience that leads to a *metanoia*</u>, is not the same thing as worldly sorrow. Worldly sorrow is the same experience of grief or distress, but the world offers no hope—only the promise of relief and death.

column4: Sorrow is also different from suffering and grief.
column5: Sorrow is also different from suffering and mourning.

column4: Suffering is the endurance of pain-physical, emotional, mental, or spiritual-especially when prolonged or intense.
column5: To suffer is to endure pain—physical, emotional, mental, or spiritual—especially when it is prolonged or severe.

column4: Grief is a multifaceted emotional response to significant personal loss, especially relational or existential.
column5: Mourning is a multidimensional emotional response to a significant personal deprivation or loss, especially of a relational or existential nature.

column4: Sorrow, suffering, and grief are closely related ideas. In the human condition we will experience all three, we can learn and grow through all three, but God will not bring about death and destruction in our lives to teach us.
column5: Grief, pain, and sorrow are closely related ideas۔ In the human condition we will experience all three، we can learn and grow through all three، but God will not bring death and destruction into our lives to teach us۔

column4: The scriptures say every good and perfect gift is from God above (James 1:17). He is a good Father who knows how to give good gifts to His children (Matthew 7:11). Godly sorrow will cause discomfort, but His discipline is just and loving. Just as a good father would not intentionally break his child’s arm to ‘teach him a lesson’, God will not inflict sickness or disease on His children to teach us.
column5: Holy Scripture says that every good and perfect gift is from above from God (James 1:17)۔ He is a good Father who knows how to give good gifts to His children (Matthew 7:11)۔ Godly grief will create unease، but His discipline is fair and loving۔ Just as a good father will not deliberately break his child’s arm to ‘teach a lesson’، in the same way God will not impose sickness or illness on His children to teach us۔

column4: A three-year-old boy was playing in the yard with his two-year-old sister. He was playing with a stick, and he intentionally hit her, causing her to cry and leaving a red mark.

column4: Their father hearing the commotion investigated and when he learned what his son did took the stick, broke it in half and tossed it away. He sent his son inside to think about what did and comforted his daughter.
column5: Their father heard the commotion and investigated and when he found out what his son had done he took the stick, broke it in two, and threw it away۔ He sent his son inside to reflect on what he had done and comforted his daughter۔

column5: God’s selfless goodness، that when we come to Him He is willing to redeem and restore us، is a positive factor on our path to repentance۔ His goodness is not that we remain engaged in sin، but that despite our sin He makes a way for us to be delivered and to experience His salvation۔

column4: ### David’s Example of Repentance
column5: ### David’s Example of Repentance

column4: Perhaps no account in the scriptures has a richer example of repentance than the story of King David’s sin found in 2 Samuel 11-12. It begins with King David remaining in Jerusalem instead of going to battle, where he sees Bathsheba bathing. Despite knowing she is the wife of Uriah, one of his loyal soldiers, David sends for her, and they have an affair, resulting in Bathsheba's pregnancy.
column5: Perhaps Scripture offers no richer example of repentance than the story of King David’s sin told in 2 Samuel 11-12. It begins with King David remaining in Jerusalem instead of going out to war, where he sees Bathsheba bathing. Even knowing that she was the wife of one of his loyal soldiers, Uriah, David sent for her, and they entered into an adulterous relationship, resulting in Bathsheba becoming pregnant.

column4: To cover his actions, David recalls Uriah from the battlefield, hoping he will spend time with Bathsheba and appear to be the child's father. However, Uriah, out of loyalty to his fellow soldiers, refuses to go to his home with Bethsheba. David then arranges for Uriah to be sent to the front lines where he is ultimately killed in battle. After Uriah's death, David hastily marries Bathsheba to cover up the pregnancy.
column5: To conceal his actions, David summoned Uriah back from the battlefield, hoping he would spend time with Bathsheba so that the child would appear to be his. But out of loyalty to his fellow soldiers, Uriah refused to go home to Bathsheba. Then David arranged for Uriah to be sent to the front lines, where he was ultimately killed in battle. After Uriah’s death, David hurriedly married Bathsheba to hide the pregnancy.

column4: The Lord is displeased with David's actions and sends the prophet Nathan to confront him. When confronted by the prophet, David immediately admitted, "*I have sinned against the Lord*" (2 Samuel 12:13). David did not try to justify or excuse his actions. This confession was the first step in his repentance, acknowledging his wrongdoing directly to God.
column5: The Lord was displeased with David’s actions and sent the prophet Nathan to rebuke him. When the prophet confronted him, David immediately confessed, “*I have sinned against the Lord*” (2 Samuel 12:13). David did not try to justify or excuse his actions. This confession was the first step in his repentance, in which he acknowledged his guilt directly before God.

column4: In Psalm 51, David’s words, “*For I know my transgressions, and my sin is always before me,*” show his complete ownership of his actions. He expresses grief not only for the sin itself but also for how it offended God, saying, “*Against you, you only, have I sinned.*” David displayed "*a broken and contrite heart,*" an essential part of true repentance (Psalms 51:17). This sorrow wasn’t superficial; he deeply grieved over the sin he committed and the hurt it caused. This depth of remorse was a sign that he wanted not only forgiveness but a changed heart.
column5: In Psalm 51, David’s words, “*For I acknowledge my transgressions, and my sin is always before me*,” show his complete responsibility for his actions. He expresses sorrow not only over the sin itself but also over having grieved God, saying, “*Against You, You only, have I sinned*.” David displayed a “*broken and contrite heart*,” which is a fundamental component of true repentance (Psalm 51:17). This sorrow was not superficial; he was deeply grieved over the sin he had committed and the harm it caused. The depth of this remorse signaled that he sought not merely forgiveness but a changed heart.

column4: David asked God to “*Create in me a pure heart, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me”* (Psalms 51:10). He sought an inner transformation that would prevent him from repeating the same mistakes. Rather than just apologizing, David pleaded with God to cleanse him, saying, “*Wash me, and I will be whiter than snow*” (Psalms 51:7). He recognized that only God could purify his heart and restore his joy.
column5: David asked God, “*Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me*” (Psalm 51:10). He wanted an inner transformation that would keep him from repeating the same mistakes. Rather than merely asking for forgiveness, David begged God to cleanse him, saying, “*Wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow*” (Psalm 51:7). He knew that only God could purify his heart and restore his joy.

column4: David’s desire to be renewed spiritually reflects a genuine commitment to walk in God’s ways moving forward. His request for a “*willing spirit*” (Psalms 51:12) demonstrates his hope to be aligned with God in every part of his life.
column5: David’s desire to be renewed spiritually reflects a genuine commitment to walk in God’s ways going forward. His request for a “*willing spirit*” (Psalm 51:12) shows that he wanted to be aligned with God in every aspect of his life.

column4: Although God put away David’s sin, the Lord struck the child and he was very sick. David fasted, prayed, and pleaded with God to spare the child, but when the child died, David accepted it (2 Samuel 12:15-23).
column5: Although God put away David’s sin, the Lord struck the child, and he became very ill. David fasted, prayed, and pleaded with God to spare the child’s life, but when the child died, David accepted it (2 Samuel 12:15-23).

column4: In Psalm 51 we find a personal prayer of repentance and a public acknowledgment of his transgressions. David’s decision to write down his plea for mercy, creating one of the Bible’s most enduring psalms, shows his willingness to be transparent about his sin and God’s forgiveness. This psalm became a testimony of repentance and restoration for others to learn from, memorializing his journey from guilt to grace.
column5: In Psalm 51 we find a personal prayer of repentance and a public confession of his transgressions. David’s decision to put his plea for mercy into writing, which produced one of the most enduring psalms in the Bible, shows that he was willing to be transparent about his sin and God’s forgiveness. This psalm became a testimony of repentance and restoration for others to learn from, memorializing his journey from guilt to grace.

column4: David’s repentance journey was not simply about feeling sorry; it was a profound change in his heart and life. Through confession, acceptance, and the heart transformation inscribed in Psalm 51, David memorialized his sin as a lesson on God’s mercy, repentance, and the possibility of restoration, making his story one of the Bible's most significant examples of genuine repentance.
column5: David’s journey of repentance did not stop at feeling sorry; it was a profound transformation of his heart and life. Through confession, acceptance, and the heart-change recorded in Psalm 51, David turned his sin into a lesson about God’s mercy, repentance, and the possibility of restoration, making his story one of the most significant examples of genuine repentance in the Bible.
